title: A weak predictor can reduce adjusted R-squared
scenario_markdown: Using the same 30 cafes and response (SST=1000), a model with advertising and price has k=2, SSR=700, SSE=300. Adding window count gives k=3, SSR=702, SSE=298. Both models have intercepts. Decide whether the small fit improvement offsets the extra predictor under adjusted R-squared.
assumptions: These are nested least-squares models on the identical response rows.
Adjusted R-squared penalizes added predictors through residual degrees of freedom.
Predictor retention may also depend on a pre-specified purpose and subject knowledge.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is ordinary R-squared after adding window count? Select the value rounded to four decimal places.

options.hint_markdown: Use the new SSR and SSE.

stages.explanation_markdown: $R_B^2=702/1000=0.7020$. An added predictor in nested OLS cannot lower ordinary R-squared. Excel: `=702/1000`.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is adjusted R-squared after adding window count? Select the value rounded to four decimal places.

options.hint_markdown: Adjusted R-squared includes a predictor penalty.
That is the adjusted value before adding the predictor.

stages.prompt_markdown: If adjusted fit is the stated criterion, what does the comparison support?

options.text_markdown: Prefer the simpler model: the small SSE decrease does not offset the loss of one residual degree of freedom.
Keep every new predictor whenever ordinary R-squared increases.
options.hint_markdown: Ordinary R-squared rewards added flexibility even when improvement is negligible.

options.text_markdown: Window count has been proved to have exactly zero population effect.
options.hint_markdown: A weak sample contribution is not proof of a zero population coefficient.

stages.explanation_markdown: Adjusted R-squared falls from 0.6778 to 0.6676. This criterion favors the simpler model, while theoretical controls or prediction goals could justify a different choice. It is not an automatic deletion rule for every setting.
